title: Hook Lines for Videos: 40 Openers That Make the Next Second Worth Watching

# Hook Lines for Videos: 40 Openers That Make the Next Second Worth Watching

At 0:02, the viewer’s thumb is already moving. Your video may be useful, beautifully edited, and completely lost because its first sentence sounded like the opening of every other video in the feed.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/NW5TFTuEOj.png)

This page gives you ready-to-use hook lines for videos, organized by what your video needs to do: challenge an assumption, name a mistake, create a useful gap, or make a specific promise. Replace the brackets with details you can support in the video itself.

## Hook lines for tutorials and how-tos

A tutorial hook should identify the result and the obstacle before the viewer has to guess either one.

1. “If your [task] keeps taking [time], start with this one change.”
2. “You do not need [popular tool] to do [result].”
3. “The fastest way I know to fix [specific problem] starts here.”
4. “Before you try [common method], check this setting.”
5. “This is the part of [task] most tutorials skip.”
6. “I made [result] in [time] using three steps.”
7. “If you are stuck at [stage], do this next.”
8. “Here is the beginner version of [advanced-looking task].”

## Hook lines for videos about mistakes

Mistake hooks work when the viewer can recognize the behavior immediately. Be precise about the moment the error happens.

9. “You are not bad at [task]. You are starting in the wrong place.”
10. “This one habit is making [problem] harder than it needs to be.”
11. “Stop doing [common action] before you check this.”
12. “The reason [desired result] is not working is probably not what you think.”
13. “Most people fix [symptom] and miss the actual problem.”
14. “If [problem] happens every time, this is the mistake to look for.”
15. “You are wasting [resource] at this exact step.”
16. “The advice to [common advice] can backfire when [condition].”

## Hook lines for videos with a contrarian angle

A contrarian hook earns attention only if the video can explain the distinction behind it. Challenge a familiar rule, then show the better rule.

17. “Stop trying to [popular goal] if you have not done this first.”
18. “You do not need more [thing]. You need a better [process].”
19. “The usual advice about [topic] misses one important condition.”
20. “Doing [popular action] every day is not always the answer.”
21. “The expensive version of [solution] is not necessarily the useful one.”
22. “More effort will not fix a broken [system].”
23. “The best time to [action] may be later than you were told.”
24. “I would not start with [obvious first step]—and here is why.”

## Hook lines for comparison videos

A comparison needs a decision, not a vague list. Name the choice and the person it is for.

25. “Choose [option A] if you need [need]; choose [option B] if you need [need].”
26. “I tested [option A] and [option B] for one job: [job].”
27. “Before you buy [product category], decide which of these two problems you have.”
28. “These look similar, but one changes [specific outcome].”
29. “The cheaper option wins when [condition].”
30. “Here is the difference between [term A] and [term B] in plain English.”
31. “If I had [budget or constraint], I would pick [option] for this reason.”
32. “Do not compare the feature lists. Compare this one use case.”

## Hook lines for stories and lessons

A story hook needs a visible turning point. Start where the plan failed, changed, or became clear.

33. “I knew [plan] was failing when [specific moment].”
34. “I spent [time] doing [action] before I noticed this pattern.”
35. “The smallest change in my [process] gave me the clearest lesson.”
36. “This was the moment I stopped treating [problem] as a motivation issue.”
37. “I expected [outcome], but [actual outcome] happened instead.”
38. “One question changed how I approach [topic].”
39. “I almost repeated the same mistake until I looked at [evidence or detail].”
40. “Here is what I would do differently on day one of [project].”

## Pick the hook that matches the video

Do not choose the most dramatic line by default. Choose the line that makes an accurate promise about the next 30 seconds.

- Use a **tutorial hook** when the viewer wants a clear action or fix.
- Use a **mistake hook** when the viewer is frustrated and may be misdiagnosing the issue.
- Use a **contrarian hook** when you can explain an exception to familiar advice.
- Use a **comparison hook** when the viewer is deciding between options.
- Use a **story hook** when a real sequence of events carries the lesson.

A good hook also matches what appears on screen. If you say, “Here is the difference,” show the two things being compared. If you say, “Stop doing this,” show the action before explaining the replacement. The spoken line, on-screen text, and first visual should all point to the same question.

## A simple way to test hook lines for videos

Write three versions before filming: one mistake hook, one question or comparison hook, and one contrarian hook. Keep the video’s core explanation the same. Then check each opener against four questions:

1. Can a stranger name the topic after hearing it once?
2. Does it promise something the rest of the video actually delivers?
3. Is there a concrete noun, action, or situation rather than a broad claim?
4. Does the on-screen text make the same promise in fewer words?

If a hook needs a long setup to make sense, it is probably a title idea rather than an opening line. Move the context into the next beat and let the first sentence carry one clean tension.

For example, “Today I want to talk about why people struggle with fitness” is a topic announcement. “Why does everyone quit by January 20th?” gives the viewer a specific problem to stay with. The second line can lead into the same lesson, but it gives the video somewhere to go.

## Turn one topic into several usable openings

Start with a narrow brief: the platform, video length, audience, topic, tone, and the claim you can demonstrate. “Hooks for a 30-second video about [topic] for [audience]” is more useful than “give me viral hooks.”

Next, ask for variations by type. One topic can support a contrarian angle, a question, a mistake, and a direct how-to. Those are different invitations for different viewer states. A beginner who feels stuck may respond to a mistake hook; someone choosing between methods may need a comparison.

Finally, script the transition. The hook is not a decorative sentence placed before the real video. Its last word should naturally lead to the next beat: the mistake, proof, demonstration, comparison, or fix.

## FAQ

### How long should a video hook be?

Use only the words needed to establish the tension or promise. A hook can be one short sentence, provided the first visual and on-screen text carry the same idea.

### Should I use a question as a hook?

Yes, when the question is specific enough that the viewer recognizes the problem. “Want better results?” is broad. “Why does everyone quit by January 20th?” identifies a moment and an audience problem.

### Can I reuse the same hook format?

Reuse a format when it fits the subject, but change the actual tension. “Stop doing this” becomes repetitive when every video hides a different, unrelated lesson behind it. Match the format to what the video proves.

### What should be on screen during the hook?

Show the object, action, result, or contrast named in the line. On-screen text should be readable without repeating every spoken word.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the kind of brief and structured result you receive:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**

  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
